title: Feed Accounting Basis: What a Ton Costs on a Feed and Animal Nutrition Programme
content:
What a ton costs is fixed by the programme's price basis. On a posted-price programme within the Feed and Animal Nutrition Programmes the price is the posted price for that class of feed on the day the load was delivered, not the day the order was taken. On a cost-plus programme the price is the cost of the ingredients in the formula on the day the mix was run plus the programme's mixing charge per ton, so two loads of the same formula a fortnight apart can carry different prices and both are right. On a contracted ingredient programme the contracted tons price at the contracted cost until they are exhausted and at the posted cost afterwards, and the two are shown as separate lines on the same invoice rather than averaged.

The money owed on an invoice for a delivered load is the tons billed multiplied by the price per ton billed, rounded to two decimal places.

## A quote given at the counter

A price quoted at the counter is held for the programme's price hold in calendar days from the day it was quoted and is requoted after that.

## What stays off the price of a ton

Bin rent, cleanout, nutritionist visits and analyses beyond the counts the programme includes are billed as their own lines and are never folded into the price per ton.

## The three bases beside one another

| Basis the programme carries | The day the price is taken from | What makes up the price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Posted price | the day the load was delivered | the posted price for that class of feed |
| Ingredient cost plus the mixing charge | the day the mix was run | the cost of the ingredients in the formula, plus the programme's mixing charge per ton |
| Contracted ingredient cost plus the mixing charge | the contracted tons at the contracted cost while they last, the rest at the posted cost | the ingredient cost on that footing, plus the programme's mixing charge per ton, carried as two lines |

*Hypothetical.* Twelve and fifty-five hundredths of a ton are billed at a price per ton of five hundred and twelve dollars and thirty-seven cents. The money owed on the invoice is the tons multiplied by that price, which comes to six thousand four hundred and thirty dollars and twenty-four cents once rounded to two decimal places.

*Hypothetical.* A contracted ingredient programme has thirty contracted tons left and a load of forty tons is run. Thirty tons stand on the invoice at the contracted cost and ten at the posted cost, as two lines, and no single blended price per ton appears for the load.
